newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin wants French defence firms to consolidate.
newsitem.headline: Jospin wants French defence firms to consolidate.

text.p: Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said on Thursday that France's defence firms must consolidate to boost competitiveness but confirmed that the former centre-right government's plans for an all-volunteer army would go ahead.

"Our (defence) enterprises must consolidate, to restore and increase their competitiveness so they can fully participate in future cooperation projects in Europe," Jospin said in a keynote policy address to the National Assembly.

"Europe is important for our defence. The government hopes to instill a new dynamism in the cooperation that will develop in this area. It is thus urgent to adopt a new and more coherent policy for the defence industries," he said.
Defence firms are threatened across Europe by shrinking military budgets and an increasingly competitive global marketplace, leading to a broad consensus for consolidation.

But consolidation plans have been put on hold in France as the new leftist government, which took power this month, has not confirmed plans to merge France's Aerospatiale with warplane maker Dassault Aviation or whether the Aerospatiale/Dassault group would then be privatised.
The Socialists have indicated hostility to privatisations.
Jospin said France required "a modern defence to keep its place in the world" and said a modernisation of the armed forces had been underway throughout the 1990s.
He said the timetable for phasing out compulsory military service for men by the year 2002, decided last year by Conservative President Jacques Chirac, "will be maintained".

But he said he wanted to take a new look at a controversial plan to summon young people to army recruitment centres for five-day "citizens' meetings" including medical tests and lessons on civic values in the event that conscription were to be needed in an emergency.
"The link uniting each citizen to the defence of his country must be better defined," he said.

The previous defence minister, conservative Charles Millon, had thought up the idea of the citizens' meetings as a way to maintain a link between French civilians and the armed forces once the military became entirely professional.

But military leaders were divided on the plan, with many branding it an expensive gimmick without military value and others saying it would prove valuable in luring youths to volunteer for the new professional army.
France has had compulsory military service for men on and off for about 200 years, but Chirac decided to phase it out because it was inefficient and unpopular among young people.
